summary: Replaces the CLI's plain 'run the EQL bundle in a transaction' install/upgrade with a protocol that, in one transaction, takes an advisory lifecycle lock, walks pg_depend for customer objects that depend on the disposable eql_v3/eql_v3_internal schemas, refuses before mutation if any is not a plain index, runs the bundle (DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE), rebuilds and verifies the captured indexes and ANALYZEs their tables. It also centralises read-only installation assessment. Versus base this is a large safety improvement: base silently cascade-dropped dependent indexes, views and policies. The data-integrity paths (rollback after DROP, refusal before mutation, upgrade from released 3.0.2 with real ciphertext) have live tests in CI jobs that passed, though per-test results were not visible. The residual release risks are operational: every EQL-indexed table is now locked for the time it takes to rebuild and analyse its indexes inside the transaction (high impact on large production tables, documented only as a generic maintenance window); the rebuild needs table ownership, which the old cascade-drop did not, so non-owner install roles now fail and roll back; previously succeeding upgrades with views/policies now refuse; and the dependency walk exempts any public operator or cast built on an EQL function, so such customer objects are still dropped silently.

behaviour_changes.description: stash eql install/upgrade now captures dependent functional indexes, replaces the EQL schemas, recreates the indexes with plain CREATE INDEX, restores cluster/replica-identity/comment/statistics settings, ANALYZEs each table and verifies the result, all in one transaction that rolls back on mismatch.

Install/upgrade now refuse, before any mutation, when a non-index object (view, policy, constraint, generated column, trigger, customer operator, partitioned index) depends on EQL machinery. At base these were silently cascade-dropped.
Lifecycle commands take a transaction-scoped advisory lock, polling for up to 300 s before failing with EqlLifecycleLockTimeoutError; JIT is disabled for the transaction.

Preflight, status, verify, install and upgrade now read installation state through assessEqlInstallation in a single read-only snapshot; preflight error wrapping and the separate ORE connection in status are gone.
CI CLI test job now runs PG16 and PG17; turbo forwards STASH_TEST_DATABASE_URL; live suites run in a single fork; a test-only npm alias of eql 3.0.2 is added with a lint exemption.
README, shipped stash-cli agent skill and changeset describe the reinstall protocol, the maintenance-window requirement and that generated migrations are unprotected.

failure_scenarios.title: Upgrade locks every EQL-indexed production table for the duration of index rebuilds and ANALYZE
failure_scenarios.trigger: An operator runs stash eql upgrade (or install --force) against a database with large tables carrying EQL functional indexes, expecting a bundle swap of roughly the old duration (the code comment puts the bundle alone at 10-30 s locally).
failure_scenarios.mechanism: The bundle's DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE drops each dependent index, which takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on its table and holds it until COMMIT (E-24). The same transaction then rebuilds every captured index with a non-concurrent CREATE INDEX evaluating an EQL function per row, applies settings and ANALYZEs each table before committing (E-1, E-2). At base the transaction ended after the bundle (E-7). No statement_timeout or lock_timeout bounds the work and nothing estimates or reports table size beforehand.
failure_scenarios.consequence: All reads and writes to those tables block for the full rebuild time (minutes to hours on large tables), an application outage; aborting rolls everything back and the work must be repeated.

existing_verification.description: Live tests exercise rebuild correctness on small fixture tables only.

missing_verification: Any measurement of lock duration or rebuild time on a populated table
Pre-flight report of which tables/indexes will be locked and rebuilt
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Have install/upgrade (and --dry-run) list the indexes and table sizes that will be rebuilt and require confirmation; state explicitly in README/skill that the tables are unavailable for the rebuild; consider an opt-in lock_timeout so a queued DROP does not stall all traffic.

failure_scenarios.title: Install role that does not own the indexed tables can no longer reinstall or upgrade
failure_scenarios.trigger: The CLI connects as a role that owns (or is a member of the owner of) the EQL schemas but not the application tables carrying EQL indexes, e.g. a dedicated migration role or a managed-platform admin role.
failure_scenarios.mechanism: At base, CASCADE dropped dependent indexes without ownership checks (E-7, E-24). Now rebuildIndexes issues CREATE INDEX and ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER ON/REPLICA IDENTITY, which need table ownership (E-2, E-24). The failure surfaces as DerivedSearchIndexReconstructionError after the DROP, and the transaction rolls back. Preflight only checks schema-drop rights (E-21). The live suite runs as the CI superuser that owns everything (E-11, E-17).
failure_scenarios.consequence: Upgrades that previously succeeded (while losing indexes) now fail after doing the expensive part of the work; the database is left on the old EQL, so a CLI/SQL version skew persists until the operator obtains table ownership.

existing_verification.description: Rollback after a failure post-DROP is live-tested, so a failed rebuild should leave the prior install intact.

missing_verification: A live test installing as a non-superuser that does not own the indexed table
A preflight check of table ownership for captured indexes
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Add table-ownership to the dependency inventory and refuse before mutation with a named remedy; add a non-owner live test.

failure_scenarios.title: Customer operator or cast in public built on an EQL function is still silently dropped
failure_scenarios.trigger: A customer has created an operator in schema public (or any cast) whose implementing function lives in eql_v3/eql_v3_internal.
failure_scenarios.mechanism: The walk exempts any public operator whose oprcode is in an EQL schema and any cast whose castfunc is in an EQL schema, classifying them as bundle-owned from the installed catalog (E-5). The bundle's CASCADE then drops them, and the incoming bundle only recreates its own. The live suite asserts a cast built that way is exempted, and covers customer operators only in a non-public schema (E-12).
failure_scenarios.consequence: A customer object disappears without a refusal, contrary to the release note that unsupported dependencies are named and refused; queries using it then fail. Not a regression versus base, which dropped it too.

existing_verification.description: Refusal table covers customer operators in a non-public schema.

missing_verification: A case for a customer operator in public, or a customer cast, over an EQL function
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Compare exempted operators/casts against the set the installed bundle version created (e.g. its expected surface) rather than exempting by implementation namespace, or document the gap.

failure_scenarios.title: Upgrades with views, policies or generated columns over EQL now refuse with no supported path forward
failure_scenarios.trigger: A customer database has an RLS policy, view, constraint, trigger or generated column referencing EQL functions, and runs stash eql upgrade after updating the CLI.
failure_scenarios.mechanism: inspectReinstallDependencies refuses any non-index dependant (E-4); install/upgrade exit 1 (E-8). --dry-run returns before the inventory so the refusal is only discovered on the real run (E-9). The documented alternative for migrations is to recreate dependants manually (E-20).
failure_scenarios.consequence: The database stays on the older EQL while the CLI/client move on; operators may fall back to raw `eql migration` SQL, which still cascade-drops the dependants silently.

failure_scenarios.mitigation: Run the dependency inventory in --dry-run and print the refusal list; document a drop/recreate procedure for each refused kind.

evidence.claim: restoreDerivedSearchIndexesAroundEqlReplacement opens one transaction, takes the advisory lifecycle lock, disables JIT, inventories dependencies, runs the full bundle (which opens with DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE), rebuilds captured indexes, then COMMITs; any error ROLLBACKs.

rebuildIndexes runs each captured pg_get_indexdef definition as a plain (non-CONCURRENTLY) CREATE INDEX, then CLUSTER ON / REPLICA IDENTITY / COMMENT / SET STATISTICS, then ANALYZE on every affected table, all inside the reinstall transaction.
The author's own comment sizes the bundle install alone at 10-30s on a local container and longer on managed Postgres; lock wait budget is 300s polled every 250ms.
Any dependent object that is not a standalone ordinary index (or an index with incomplete metadata) raises EqlReinstallRefusalError before the bundle runs.

Dependency walk exempts any operator in schema public whose implementing function is in eql_v3/eql_v3_internal, and any cast whose function is in those schemas, regardless of who created the operator or cast.

EQLInstaller.install now delegates to restoreDerivedSearchIndexesAroundEqlReplacement; typed refusal/lock/connection errors are rethrown unchanged, others are wrapped as 'Failed to install EQL ... rolled back'.
At base, install() ran BEGIN; bundledSql; COMMIT with no dependency inventory and no index reconstruction, so CASCADE silently dropped dependent indexes, views, policies etc.
stash eql install renders EqlReinstallRefusalError as an expected failure (CliExit(1)); other errors propagate.

The DDL issued here is subject to PostgreSQL semantics not verified in this repository: CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER ON / REPLICA IDENTITY require ownership of the table, while DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE removes dependent objects without checking ownership of each dependant; non-concurrent CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock, and the cascade-drop of an index takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on its table until commit.
